body:
Why Europeans Entered Indian Ocean Trade

Indian textiles and Asian spices were valuable commodities in European markets. European merchants sought direct access to the Indian Ocean trading system in order to purchase goods and sell them at a profit.

The Portuguese were the earliest of the major European maritime powers to establish a sustained presence on the western coast of India. Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 after sailing around the Cape of Good Hope. Calicut was on the Malabar Coast, not in Gujarat.

The Portuguese subsequently established important positions on India's western coast, including Goa. Their naval activities affected the conditions under which other merchants operated in the Arabian Sea.

European Companies at Surat

In 1600, Queen Elizabeth I granted a charter to the English East India Company. The charter gave it exclusive rights against competing English trading groups for trade with the East. It did not prevent Portuguese, Dutch or other European merchants from operating in Asian markets.

During the 17th century, Portuguese, Dutch and English traders maintained commercial establishments at Surat. The French East India Company established a factory at Surat in 1668.

Factory in early European trade

A factory was a trading establishment containing offices and often warehouses. Its employees, called factors, arranged purchases, sales and shipments. It was not necessarily a place where goods were manufactured by machines.

Indian Merchants and European Companies

When European companies expanded their commercial activities, they entered markets already served by Indian merchants, bankers, brokers and shipowners.

Prominent Surat merchants such as Virji Vora and Mulla Abdul Ghafur illustrate the continuing importance of Indian commercial activity. European companies needed access to Indian goods, and they often dealt with local merchants and financial intermediaries.

Competition among European companies could increase the prices paid for desirable goods. Over time, the companies also used shipping strength, naval force and control over commercial routes to improve their position. Their commercial rivalry increasingly had political consequences.

How Company Trade Affected Textile Producers

European demand encouraged the expansion of textile production. More artisans became involved in spinning, weaving, bleaching and dyeing.

Company agents also used advances to secure cloth before production was complete. A weaver who accepted such an arrangement might have to supply a particular quantity or design of cloth to the purchaser. This could reduce the craftsperson's freedom to sell the finished product to someone else.

These changes developed gradually. The presence of a European factory at a port did not automatically mean that the company controlled the surrounding territory.

Why Surat's Relative Importance Declined

Surat's commercial difficulties developed towards the end of the 17th century and became more serious during the 18th century. Several causes contributed:

  • Weakening Mughal authority: Political insecurity and disruptions in the hinterland made the movement of goods more difficult.
  • Disruption of West Asian commercial connections: Difficulties affecting Persian Gulf and Red Sea markets reduced opportunities for trade.
  • European maritime competition: Growing European control over shipping and sea routes changed the position of Indian merchants.
  • Rise of Bombay: Bombay, present-day Mumbai, became an increasingly important centre of English East India Company trade and competed with Surat.
  • Port conditions: Silting and navigational disadvantages also affected Surat's ability to compete with other harbours.

Surat did not suddenly become an abandoned port. Trade continued there even as Bombay gained relative importance. The decline of a port's dominance is different from the complete disappearance of commercial activity.

The Complete Commercial Relationship

Medieval Gujarat's merchant networks can be understood as a connected system. Artisans and agricultural producers supplied commodities. Markets in Ahmedabad, Bharuch and other inland centres gathered and distributed goods. Roads connected these markets with Cambay and Surat. Merchants, brokers and shipowners organised transactions and transport, while shroffs and hundis helped arrange credit and payment. Indian Ocean routes linked Gujarat with West Asia, East Africa, Southeast Asia and China. European companies subsequently joined and increasingly competed within these networks.

Prelims focus

  • Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, not Surat.
  • The English East India Company received its charter in 1600 from Queen Elizabeth I.
  • The French East India Company established a factory at Surat in 1668.
  • A European trading factory was an office and warehouse establishment, not necessarily a manufacturing plant.
  • Surat's relative decline involved several causes, including Mughal weakening, changing overseas trade and competition from Bombay.
  • Trap: The arrival of a European trading company did not immediately establish European territorial rule over Gujarat.
